text: — And what about you, Dravichka, why are you silent, don't you know something about Bai Ganyo? — asked one of the company our cheerful friend Dravichka.
— How could I not know, brother, I know a great deal of things, but how can one tell them? — Dravichkata answers with feigned modesty.
— How you will tell them! If only I had your mouth!
— Well then, listen:

I went one summer for a stroll in Geneva, you know it, in Switzerland. I took a room in a hotel and went out to walk around the city. The city — beautiful, the surroundings — both picturesque and majestic. I was walking like that, aimlessly, staring left and right, and from street to street I came out onto the square where the opera house is. I saw an elegant café opposite: wait, I said to myself, let me stop by to rest a bit. To the right of the entrance, I saw a glass partition with an open view of the square and I went in — I would drink coffee and watch who passed by at the same time. And what did I find there! Three whole tables occupied by Bulgarian students! Well, go ahead and say that Bulgarians have no taste for elegance! In such a beautiful city, in the best part of town, in the most elegant café, they had taken the best spot! Noise, smoke, matches and smoking cigarettes on the floor, clattering, shouting, brawls!... Here they play backgammon, there preference, over there trenta una!... And I hear from all sides: “Shesh-besh!... Hearts!... Give me the money! Jehar-i-yek!... Why are you looking at my cards, man!... Garçon!... First to the second!... Du-besh!... You're lying, it's not du-besh!... Trenta una... Spades!... Garçon!... You haven't a clue about preference!... I don't want advice from socialists!... Dubara!... And I don't want advice from chorbadzhii!... I trump!... Scoundrel!... Garçon! Are you proud of your decorations?... Clubs!... And what about you and the Russian kikes? Gentlemen, the fool is coming! Ha, ha, ha!... Garçon un chope! Give me another franc as a loan, man!... You're a deadbeat! Borrow from the waiter!... Dort-jehar!...”

The individual to whom they had attached the not-so-flattering epithet "fool" entered the café and greeted the students, who welcomed him, as the saying goes, with open arms; he did not know which group to join, as those at every table were trying to attract him. Such sympathy toward a fool seemed inexplicable to me at first, but before long, my bewilderment dissipated through the words exchanged across the tables at this person's expense. Later, I learned that this "fool" was the son of a landowner from Argentina, in South America. A wealthy boy. His father sent him 500 francs a month, half of which was distributed every month into the pockets of our students with the help of *trenta una*. And because he good-naturedly allowed himself to be fleeced, while taking pleasure in observing the greed—so curious to him—with which our lot lured away his money, he was honored with the title "fool."

At whatever hour of the day I visited this café, starting from 9 o'clock in the morning until late in the evening, I constantly found the same faces at the same occupations — backgammon, preference, trenta una. When these young men read, in what way they assimilated European culture — this remained inexplicable to me. It was clear to me only that almost none of them spoke the French language passably. No sooner would he open his mouth in this language, and by the coarseness of the intonation, by the diction, by the construction of the phrases, you would recognize that he was an Eastern man.

Every day or two, this company was joined by several embittered, nihilistic young Jews, who from the dark corners of the taverns bared their teeth at the tyrant. I do not know what this sympathy was for these dark heroes, who are capable of being simultaneously nihilists, secret police agents, anarchists, and the lowest sort of embezzlers of society funds, libraries, and other properties. Instead of associating with the French, the Germans, the English—always exemplary both in their revelries and in their pursuits—instead of imbuing themselves with their spirit of decency, industriousness, honesty, and chivalry, they, our people, found their ideal either in the young Jews, or the young Greeks, or some young Armenians, who in the basest manner exploited their means and energies, drawing them into the stifling atmosphere of their malicious, crude, and fruitless rantings. Later I learned that in this city there were other young Bulgarians who did not frequent this café, but occupied themselves most seriously with their studies.
One day, at the height of trenta una, when the Argentine had lost about a hundred francs, a person entered the cafe with a tilted fur hat, a staff under his arm, and saddlebags in hand.
— Oh! Bay Ganyo! Welcome! — the whole company shouted.

— Glad to find you well! How are you? — the newcomer replied, and magnanimously declining the polite offers to make room for him at their tables, he came and sat at my table, and as he sat down, he knocked over my cup of coffee. A swaggering nature!
— Pardon!
"— It’s nothing, don’t worry," I hastened to say, even though I hadn't noticed him being particularly worried.
— Ah! Are you Bulgarian? Well, good day then! Ganyo Balkanski! Where are you from, your honor?
I told him. We met.
— With this wretched rose oil I travel the world — Bay Ganyo told me in a desperate voice.
— What, isn't this trade going well?
— Well, to tell you the truth, sir, it's not going well!
— Why so?

— Why! We suffer from our own doing. Once upon a time—when you said Bulgarian oil, they would come running like wasps to honey, but now, what a world! You walk into some soap shop, and before you can even open your mouth to say you're Bulgarian, whether you've said "bonjour" or not, he up and asks you "Essence de rose?"—and he asks while smirking. And who cares about the smirking, as long as there's business to be done, but they don't want it! "Give me," he says, "one gram for a sample." He's mocking you! How can you give him one gram? You'll pour one gram—and spill two. "But, my friend," I tell him, "this oil isn't what you think it is, this is pure oil." — "Aha," he says, "you all say the same thing, you're all singing the same tune." — He says it to you like that, right to your face, he doesn't want to know you at all. But it's all that cursed adulterant, damn it to hell!... Anatolia has been our ruin! Well, brother, it's not just one or two: they've swarmed across Europe in droves: Anatolians, Armenians, Turks, Greeks, and they lie, and they cheat the world, and they've burned this one, and they've swindled that one—people are fed up! As soon as they catch a whiff of rose from you—they're on their guard!...
The innocent East stood out before me with all its charms. To complete the picture, backgammon boards clattered and cards slapped at all the tables around us—noise and smoke reaching the heavens!

— I really like our boys — Bai Ganyo told me, looking over the players. — Fine fellows! There are some among them so bold that they could teach the professors a thing or two! Take, for instance, let’s say, that boy, the older one, do you see him? The one playing otuz-bir. Do you know that he has three medals!... For the Serbian war, for merit, and I don’t know what else. He was a judicial investigator; he knows the laws like the back of his hand. Why he even needed to study more, who knows — his money must be burning a hole in his pocket! It’s been three months since he arrived here, but you should hear him, he rattles off French like a house on fire! Touch wood, he’s got a sharp head on his shoulders! He would have become a doctor by now, but the people here are stubborn. The Rector, he says, won't let him. It’s not possible, he says, he told him, to become a doctor in three months, he says. Well, how can it not be possible when the boy knows his stuff; if you stood him up right now, he’d recite all the laws to you, he knows them by heart. The Rector told him, it’s not possible, he says, to even read them all in three months, let alone learn them. Our bold fellow — no, I’ll become a doctor in three months. The other one — no, it’s not allowed. — Not allowed? — Not allowed! Then one day our fellow flares up and gives him such a dressing down, he made a complete fool of him... Really, there, ask him if you like... I took Bai Ganyo’s word for it and did not go to ask the holder of the three medals.

He continued: — And do you know how that business went down? Not only did the rector get stubborn and wouldn't let the boy become a doctor, but the dean, he says, him too. Your Honor, you know what a “dean” is... that thing, over there with them... that sort of thing... you get it... Our man presented them with a pile of certificates — whether from the city council, or from the prosecutor, and a service record, and what not. But does a stubborn man listen? And it's not like he's just any kid, he's a judicial investigator! And with three medals on his chest, if you please!... The rector started blathering to him that in order to be useful to himself and his people — what business is it of his! — he had to regularly complete a full course, and that living abroad for a longer time would be to his benefit — the fool! — and many such old wives' tales. And never mind the rector, but — like a meddling fool — the dean speaks up too: “Yes, he says, I also recommend that you follow the rector's advice!” Hey! Then our man's temper flared up, and he barked: “And you — he says — why are you speaking up, are you going to be the rector's lawyer or what!...” He blurted that out to the dean! — Those people tucked their tails, they couldn't say a peep!... Hey, garçon! Un café!... No, say what you will, Your Honor, but we have sharp boys. Bravo!...
— Waiter, hey! A coffee! — shouted Bay Ganyo.
— Monsieur! — the nimble waiter responded.
— Un café et apporte gazette bulgare — ordered Bay Ganyo and then, turning to me, added: — I haven't forgotten them, these French rascals.
The waiter brought him coffee and some stained covers, in which several Bulgarian newspapers, frayed at the edges, were attached.

— "Wait, let's see what news there is, what's going on in the world," said Bai Ganyo, as he unfolded the covers and delved into politics. I watched from the side how he greedily, with relish, devoured the short articles, smiling and, with eyes alight, letting out a "bravo!" every now and then. At one point, seemingly overflowing with admiration, he turned to me:
— Oh, how they've messed them up! Listen, let me read to you...
— Excuse me, Mr. Balkanski, at least here I want to give my ears a rest from this politics — I said and rose from my chair, — farewell!
— But just listen to this: “That brigand rabble of pimps, thieves, and scoundrels, who stick their snouts into the filth...” Wait, it gets even better further on!...
— No, no! Farewell, Mr. Balkanski — I cried out decisively and left.
